title: How can you practise case interviews on your own?
description: A practical routine for building case interview skills alone: what you can practise solo, a 30-minute daily plan and how to do a full case by yourself.
hook: You can practise most of a case interview on your own: structuring, maths, charts, market sizing, fit stories and your delivery all improve with short solo sessions, as long as you speak out loud, time yourself and check your work against a model answer. What solo practice cannot fully give you is a live person interrupting and pushing back, so add partner cases once you can finish a case alone. Here is a daily routine, a method for running a full case by yourself, and how to give yourself feedback that actually changes something.
body:
In this guide

  • What you can build on your own
  • A 30-minute daily routine
  • How to run a full case by yourself
  • A worked solo session
  • How to give yourself useful feedback
  • Mistakes people make practising alone
  • When to add a partner
  • Check yourself

What you can build on your own

A case is a bundle of separate skills. Most of them can be trained alone, in short bursts, with quick feedback.

SkillSolo exerciseFeedback
StructuringTwo-minute structures for a written promptCompare with a model answer
MathsShort sums, said out loudCheck against the answer and your time
ChartsOne chart, insight in one sentenceCompare with the model insight
Market sizingOne estimate a dayCompare logic and a cross-check
Fit storiesWrite, then tell each in two minutesRecord and play back
Delivery60-second recommendationsRecord, count filler words, re-record

The common thread is speaking. Silent practice feels productive but hides the problems that appear the moment you talk: losing your place in a calculation, rambling, saying "um" before every point.

A 30-minute daily routine

  1. 5 minutes: a voice or thinking warm-up from the daily exercises.
  2. 10 minutes: three structuring prompts from a practice set such as the profitability set, or the structuring drill. Two minutes to structure each, then compare.
  3. 10 minutes: mental maths or one sizing question, out loud.
  4. 5 minutes: say one recommendation out loud and record it. Play it back once.

Thirty minutes a day, five days a week, is 150 minutes of focused practice. That beats a single exhausting weekend session because you get feedback daily and fix things while they are fresh.

How to run a full case by yourself

Full cases matter because they test whether you can link the skills together. You can do them alone if you are disciplined about not peeking.

  1. Choose a case with hidden data. Every case in the PrepForCase casebook reveals its exhibits step by step, so you only see data when you would have asked for it.
  2. Talk as if someone is listening. Recap the prompt out loud, state your clarifying questions and then read the answers.
  3. Draw your structure on paper before you look at anything else. Say where you would start and why.
  4. Ask for data before you reveal it. Say what you want and why. If the case gives you something else, notice the difference: that is where your structure missed something.
  5. Do every calculation out loud, on paper, with units written next to each number.
  6. Close with a 60-second recommendation, recorded on your phone.
  7. Only then read the model answer.

It feels strange the first few times. It works.

A worked solo session

Set a 35-minute timer and split it like this: 3 minutes to understand the prompt, 4 to structure, 15 for data and calculations, 3 to record a recommendation and 10 to review.

Say the prompt is: "A regional bus operator's on-time rate has fallen from 90% to 80%. The transport authority wants it back above 90% within a year." You can write a prompt like this yourself; use a casebook case when you want realistic data.

Structure (4 minutes). Delays come from the road (traffic, roadworks), the stop (boarding time, ticketing), the bus (breakdowns) and the timetable (unrealistic running times). Hypothesis: a few routes with roadworks explain most of it.

Numbers (15 minutes). The operator runs 2,000 trips a day. At 90% on time, 200 are late; at 80%, 400 are. So there are 200 extra late trips a day. Suppose the data shows two routes out of 40 account for 120 of those extra 200. That is 60% of the problem on 5% of the routes.

Recommendation (3 minutes). "Focus on the two worst routes first. They cause 60% of the extra delays. Retime their timetables around the roadworks and add bus priority where the council allows it. Fixing those alone would cut late trips from 400 to 280 a day, an on-time rate of 86%, so we also need a second fix across the network, such as contactless-only boarding to cut dwell times."

Review (10 minutes). Covered next.

How to give yourself useful feedback

Feedback is the ingredient most solo practice lacks. Before you read any model answer, play back your recording and write down three things:

  • One missed branch. "I never asked whether delays were concentrated by time of day."
  • One maths slip or slow step. "I hesitated converting 80% of 2,000."
  • One moment you gave a number without saying what it meant.

Then compare with the model answer and add anything it reveals. Finally, re-record only the opening and the close. They are the parts interviewers remember, and they are the fastest to improve.

Specific beats general. "My analysis was weak" cannot be acted on. "I never asked whether delays were concentrated on two routes" can. Keep a running list and read your last five fixes before every new case.

Mistakes people make practising alone

  • Reading the answer too early. If you look at the model structure before drawing your own, you learn nothing about your gaps.
  • Practising silently. Thinking a case through in your head is not the same skill as saying it.
  • Only choosing comfortable case types. Keep a rough tally and push yourself into the types you avoid.
  • No time limit. Real cases are timed. Without a clock you will structure for eight minutes and never notice.
  • Never moving on to people. Solo practice builds the foundations; it does not test you under pressure.

When to add a partner

Practising alone builds skill. Practising with someone builds comfort under pressure: being interrupted, being asked "why?", getting data you did not expect. Once you can complete a full case alone in about 30 minutes, add at least a few cases with another person before the real interview. They do not need a business background. Every casebook case comes with an interviewer script, so a friend can read it out and reveal exhibits on cue. Practising with a partner explains how to run those sessions and give feedback.

Check yourself

1. You have 20 minutes today. What do you do?

Show the answer

Pick your weakest skill and drill it: three timed structures, or ten minutes of out-loud maths plus one chart read, then a recorded 60-second recommendation. Short and targeted beats a rushed full case.

2. In the bus example, the two worst routes were fixed completely and late trips fell from 400 to 280. What is the new on-time rate, and how many more late trips must go to reach 90%?

Show the answer

280 late out of 2,000 is 14% late, so 86% on time. To reach 90%, late trips must fall to 200, so another 80 a day must go.

3. Your review note says "be clearer". Rewrite it.

Show the answer

Make it a behaviour you can check: "Start every answer with the conclusion, then give the reasons," or "Say 'I have three points' before listing them."

Where to go next

Fit solo practice into a schedule with the one-week, three-week or six-week plan, and start today with the four short drills.
